Once Kendall is gone, Taylor and Christy head to Terminal Dock to retrieve the suitcase. They find the $2 million intact, as well as clothing with tailor labels bearing the names Larry Cravat and "W. George, tailor". Taylor realizes he is Larry Cravat, and that after the Steele murder, he must have taken on a new identity and then enlisted in the U.S. Marines to hide. He shows the unsigned letter to Christy, who verifies that it was written by Mary after Cravat abandoned her. Taylor and Christy then come under fire from an unseen assailant and hide in a soup kitchen. Taylor has the soup kitchen's manager take the suitcase to Lt. Kendall.
Taylor and Christy are forcibly brought before Anzelmo, who demands his meeting with Cravat, but Phillips arrives with a gun and helps Taylor and Christy escape with him to The Cellar. It dawns on Taylor that Phillips is Steele's murderer. Phillips confirms this and clarifies what happened in 1942. Steele had struck a deal with Phillips to launder the Nazi money, but Cravat got wind of the exchange, passed himself off as Phillips, and took the money from Steele. Phillips arrived to find Steele empty-handed and shot him, believing he had been cheated, but then noticed Cravat running away and deduced that Cravat had the money. Phillips was also behind Michael Conroy's murder, the truck that almost hit Taylor, and the gunman at the dock. As Phillips threatens to kill Christy, Taylor offers to show him where the Nazi money is stashed and leads him to the soup kitchen. Once there, Lt. Kendall appears and shoots Phillips to disarm him; upon receiving the suitcase earlier, Kendall had placed the soup kitchen under police surveillance. Phillips is hospitalized and makes a full confession to the police, and Anzelmo's crew is rounded up. Taylor and Christy set out to start a new life together.
story_text_b:
A soldier wakes up in a hospital in the Pacific during the war. Despite the severe injuries caused by a mine explosion, the only problem that remains is his amnesia.
The doctors identify him as George Taylor although he retains only a small hint of his identity, the unsigned letter from a woman who seems to explain the hatred towards him. Frightened by what he intuits that may mean in relation to his past, he will follow any lead until he discovers his true identity.[2]

story_text_a:
Seventeen-year-old Simon lives quietly with his family and is a senior at a nearby high school. He spends his free time with his friends Leah, Abby and Nick. Simon, however, hasn't revealed his biggest secret to anyone: being gay.
She's been exchanging e-mails with a mysterious gay boy named Blue for some time, who she falls in love with and writes to all the time, trying to figure out who he is. One day, he uses a computer in the school library to check his e-mail box, but in order not to let his math teacher read the e-mails, he hastily shuts down the computer and leaves.
Martin, his classmate, uses the computer after him and, turning it on, finds himself reading Simon's emails, of which he takes screenshots. Martin then decides to blackmail Simon, threatening to publish the messages if he did not help him win over Abby, who, however, does not deserve Martin even a glance, since she is in love with Nick. Simon agrees, fearing that if the emails become public, Blue will stop writing to him.
Simon, meanwhile, continues his quest to find out who Blue really is. Many clues lead to Bram, a boy in his class, but after seeing him at a party with a girl, his illusions crumble. Leah, Simon's best friend, is also trying to get him to understand that she has feelings for him, but the boy thinks that her phrases about love are aimed at Nick.
At school, meanwhile, the kids are working on a musical that Simon and Abby and Martin are also working on. Simon then decides to go with the two comrades to a fast food restaurant to go over the jokes. Here he meets a waiter his former classmate, Lyle, who suspects him to be Blue and thus revives in Simon the hope of having found him.
Meanwhile, Simon convinces Leah to go out with Nick.
Some time later the protagonist decides to talk to Abby about his homosexuality, inspired by Blue's words in an email, but is struck by the fact that his friend is not particularly surprised.
The next night Leah, Nick, Simon and Abby decide to go to the school football game and here Simon meets Lyle, who nevertheless insinuates an interest in Abby. So the hope of finding Blue collapses once again. Before the start of the game, during the national anthem, Martin proposes to Abby in front of everyone, but receives a rejection. This leads to constant mockery of the boy, who decides to publish the e-mails to distract everyone from himself. Within minutes, all the students learn of Simon's homosexuality, including his younger sister Nora and friends. Leah, Nick and Abby are very angry with Simon because he tried to get in the way of their love affairs to get what he wanted. During lunch time some boys start making fun of Simon for being gay and his friends start to realize the mood of their friend, although they remain very angry with him. In a confrontation with Martin, Simon berates him for denying him the right to speak out himself about his homosexuality in his own time and with the people who really matter to him. Also, Blue, frightened by the outcry, has cut off all contact with Simon.
On Christmas Day, Simon admits to being gay in front of his parents, who, especially his father, are impressed. Meanwhile, the protagonist thinks he has finally found Blue, when he re-reads the emails and finds a sentence from the mysterious boy saying that he has to leave with his father to a house in the woods. Simon then remembers a fellow actor who was due to leave, Cal, but is once again disappointed when he denies being Blue.
Simon then decides to write a post on the site where his emails ended, in which he apologizes to his friends for his behavior and tells publicly about when Blue told him to feel on a Ferris wheel, because one moment he is the king of the world and the next in the abyss. Simon also tells Blue that if he finally wants to say who he is, he can meet him at the amusement park on the Ferris wheel after the show. Leah, Nick, and Abby reconcile with Simon, and they all escort their friend to the rendezvous point. After several rounds, hopes of meeting Blue diminish with each passing day. After running out of tickets, Martin arrives, apologizes to Simon, and pays his friend for more rides. That's when Blue arrives, who turns out to be Bram. The two climb the Ferris wheel together, and when they reach the top, they kiss passionately. Simon then asks Bram why he was with a girl on the night of the party and he replies that it was because of the alcohol and the lack of sobriety he had at the time.
The next morning the group, now made up of five friends, goes to school, much more united and serene than before.
story_text_b: Fred Jones (Ewan McGregor) is an expert member of the National Center for Fish Farming Promotion and has Asperger's syndrome. When consultant Harriet Chetwode-Talbot (Emily Blunt), who represents a wealthy Yemeni sheikh (Amr Waked), asks for help in fulfilling the sheikh's vision of introducing salmon fishing in the desert country of Yemen, Fred rejects the idea as unfeasible. However, the Prime Minister's press secretary, Patricia Maxwell (Kristin Scott Thomas), welcomes it as a story of "goodwill" Anglo-Arab cooperation to distract voters from the developing bad news about Afghanistan and presses Fred to work with Harriet and the sheikh to get the project off the ground. Little by little he's starting to believe in finding the sheik. Away from his wife for whom his career is everything, Fred falls in love with Harriet, whose boyfriend, Robert (Tom Mison), has just disappeared in combat. After Fred declares his love for Harriet, Robert returns alive, so he must choose between the two men. The fish are released and the project seems to yield good results, but is sabotaged by local militants, who destroy the salmon. But when Fred sees that some fish have survived, his faith is restored and Harriet joins him in fulfilling the sheik's vision.

story_text_a: U.S. Marshals Pete Nessip and his brother Terry are boarding a Boeing 747, escorting Earl Leedy, a rogue computer scientist who leaked top-secret drug-trafficking information to the underworld. In the middle of the flight, a pirate commando hijacks the plane. In the ensuing shootout, Terry is wounded and sucked into the void. The hijackers blow a door off the plane and parachute out with Leedy. On the sidelines, Pete leads the investigation by getting himself accepted into a group of paratroopers. He hopes to find those who killed his brother and put an end to their criminal activities.
story_text_b:
A government prisoner, Earl Leedy, a renegade computer expert who was being escorted by federal agent Pete Nessip and his brother, manages to parachute out of the plane transporting him to a federal prison, aided by his reckless and dangerous cohort of henchmen led by Ty Moncrief, a corrupt former DEA agent. Pete Nessip tries with his brother to stop the escape, but fails and in that escape his brother and several passengers are also killed.
After the tragedy, the authorities investigate the incident and do not believe their version of events. They believe that the perpetrators were terrorists who wanted to hijack the plane and it went wrong, so there was damage to the plane and they died, including Leedy and his brother, something they wanted to ride like that so they could escape and stay undercover. He is therefore temporarily removed from service, as they partially blame him and his brother for what happened, because they assume that their actions contributed to the tragedy.
However, Pete is determined to win back Leedy and his reputation and avenge his brother's death. So he's determined to apprehend the killers, who now use his services to infiltrate the DEA and steal data on their informants for the purpose of selling them to drug traffickers for a lot of money, thus causing the deaths of several of them. In time you will realize that this was the work of expert paratroopers who were trained by Jagger, a great expert paratrooper and who killed him so that they could erase their tracks after what they did. He eventually receives help from Jessie Crossman, an expert parachutist, who is also determined to stop them when she learns what has happened.
With his help, you can infiltrate the world of paratroopers and find out who they are and what they've done. Additionally they discover they want to raid the DEA again with the same intent but on a larger scale. They're determined to stop them for everything they've done and want to do by killing most of them. They also manage to catch Leedy again and thus achieve their purposes.

story_text_a:
In a research laboratory in Florida, scientists are trying to teach dolphins to speak.
They work with two dolphins, named Ivan (Fa) and Bessie (Bi). After the scientists succeed in mating the two together, the dolphins begin to talk. For the scientists, this is a very big breakthrough, but scientist Michael has moral concerns about the project. He fears that the dolphins could be used for military purposes and believes that the ongoing Vietnam War is unjustified, which is why he is called a communist.
There's a big press conference where the dolphins talk to the reporters. Fa explains to reporters that he can also read and his favorite book is "The Jungle Book". Fa compares himself to the figure of Mowgli, since he was raised by humans.
But one day, Fa and Bi are kidnapped and a nuclear explosion destroys an American cruiser off the coast of China. World War III is about to break out.
story_text_b: Through the lives of three women named Lucia (played by Raquel revuelta-Lucia I, Eslinda Núñez-Lucia II and Adela Legrá-Lucia III) we observe three important stages in the history of Cuba (War of Independence, opposition to the dictatorship of Gerardo Machado, Castro Revolution)

story_text_a: Lucas, a recently divorced kindergarten teacher, is suddenly accused of pedophilia. Gradually, the mistrust of the locals and his former friends gives way to a real witch hunt, and rumors spread like wildfire. A real descent into hell for him and his family begins.
story_text_b:
Newspaper reporter Pete (Bing Crosby) works in a Paris orphanage. His charming way with children and music enables him to find homes for even the most troubled kids. One afternoon, Mr. and Mrs. Godfrey (Alan Reed and Minna Gombell), an American couple, come to the orphanage to adopt Bobby, a boy they saw in one of the ads Pete ran in his newspaper. Bobby misbehaves, but when Pete discovers that Mr. Godfrey plays for the Boston Symphony Orchestra, he quickly produces a young blind opera wunderkind, Theresa (Anna Maria Alberghetti), who sings her way into the Godfreys' hearts.
Later that night, Pete dreams that the fiancée he left behind in America, Emmadel (Jane Wyman) has visited. She appears in a hologram atop his record player, scolding him for leaving her at the altar and talks about the children they might have had. Filled with regret, Pete arranges to adopt both Bobby and his little sister Suzi and bring them to Boston, where he'll marry Emmadel. American authorities inform him that he must marry within five days or the adoption will be void.
After delays in obtaining the children's birth certificates, they and Pete finally fly to Boston, and go to Emmadel's house. While she bonds with Bobby and Suzi, Pete discovers that Emmadel is engaged to an aristocratic man, Wilbur Stanley, whose office she works in. She had gotten tired of waiting for Pete's arrival home. The kids stay with her loud parents (drunken father James Barton, a fisherman, and disapproving mother Connie Gilchrist). Pete tries everything to win Emmadel back. She helps him secure a lease on a new house via her fiancé's company. However, when Pete and the children arrive at the house in the rain, they discover that another couple (the McGonigles) also have a lease for the property. Emmadel's fiancé Wilbur shows up to settle the matter. Wilbur offers Pete a ride to another house - but Pete talks him into letting them stay at the Stanley family's gatehouse. They agree to a friendly competition for Emmadel's heart during the few days leading up to the wedding.
Pete and the children settle into the Stanleys' lavish gatehouse, where Emmadel's parents are also staying. Emmadel meets Wilbur's amiable elderly relatives, who present her with $500,000 as a wedding gift. Her parents embarrass her by running screaming through the garden. Emma discovers Pete's presence and visits the gatehouse to have it out with him. After she pulls Suzi's loose tooth, Pete pretends to be in love with Winnifred, Wilbur's fourth cousin twice-removed, and laughs when Emmadel pratfalls on her huge party dress.
Pete reveals his plan to Winnifred Stanley. He discovers that she has long been in love with her cousin Wilbur, but feels too socially awkward to pursue him. In a bit of Pygmalion, Pete teaches Winnifred to feel comfortable with herself. Winnifred's newfound confidence bubbles over at the wedding rehearsal. She and Emmadel erupt in a brawl on the front lawn. Winnifred concedes the fight, and Emmadel declares that she's proud to be a fisherman's daughter.
The wedding day arrives. News reporters line the outdoor chapel, proclaiming this the Cinderella story of the decade. As he escorts Emma down the aisle, Pa Jones tells her that Pete kidnapped the children and ran so they wouldn't be sent back to France. Emmadel begins to have second thoughts. Pete shows up at precisely the wrong moment, handcuffed to a policeman, with both crying kids in tow. Although Wilbur offers to marry Emma and adopt the children, Bobby and Suzi cling sobbing to Pete. On national television, Wilbur abandons his own wedding and forces a reluctant Emma and a protesting (but secretly thrilled) Pete to marry. Pete, Emmadel, Bobby, Suzi, Ma and Pa Jones all ride off for their honeymoon together.

story_text_a:
# Foreword and introduction
In the foreword, Holbach replies to the alleged letter of a reader, who on the one hand agrees with the criticism of Christian beliefs, but on the other hand argues that the common people need a religion, since otherwise they would not be deterred by anything from crimes. Holbach replies that it is not religion but laws that restrain the people, and therefore asks the critic whether he belongs to those "petty thinkers" "who think that the truth can harm". Everything indicates that the preface is addressed to Voltaire, and that Holbach wanted to refute his predictable objections to the contents of the book from the outset.
Holbach makes it clear in the introduction that the worship of a god should not be based on the expectation of reward or punishment from that god. Rather, man must use reason to investigate the causes of his desires and fears, and few are willing to do so. Individuals, whether rich or poor, cling to the faith only because they have been brought up and taught that way from childhood; in this way religious views could have endured for centuries:
Because of its role as a model for its God, who is portrayed as cruel and wicked, the Christian religion has brought nothing but hatred, division and violence to the people. Nor would kings and rulers have gained anything from Christianity, since they would have had to submit to the priesthood again and again. This makes it all the more important to unveil the veil of Christianity and examine its principles.
# History and origin of the Judeo-Christian religions (Chapters 2 and 3)
The history of the Jewish and Christian religions is described by the author briefly and in dry words; the aim pursued by Fontenelle (De lorigine des fables) and Boulanger (Lantiquité dévoilée), to reveal the human-psychological causes of beliefs through a historical analysis, interests him only marginally. Holbach presents the origin of the Jewish people in a small area, hardly noticed by the other peoples, as emphatically banal and meaningless, in order to deny it any credibility. To the unpromising starting position of this people add their superstition and ignorance. Moses had turned the Hebrews into "possessed and ferocious monsters" who hated other gods and who, as reported in the First Book of Kings, acted barbarically against other nations. As slaves of various peoples, the Jews had  always been a victim of their credulity  been treated harshly and  deservedly  before becoming even more fanatical under Roman domination. These were the circumstances, according to Holbach's anti-Jewish portrayal of the Old Testament, under which the Jewish people were expecting their Messiah.
The origin of Christianity is described in a similarly sober and sometimes sarcastic tone. A poor Jew suddenly appeared, convinced an ignorant crowd that he was the Son of God, and was eventually executed by the other Jews. Holbach emphasizes the Egyptian, Phoenician, Platonic, and other influences of the new "blunt and incoherent" religion - a theme that is addressed again and again in the following chapters. At first, only the poor among the Jews and Gentiles would have felt addressed by a God who was hostile to the rich and powerful. Only the Roman emperors, who may or may not have converted to Christianity, would have helped the church to gain independence and eventually supremacy. The contrast between the love of neighbor preached by Christians and their fanatical cruelty is explained by the adoption of the Jewish God, whose terrible nature was aggravated by the concept of eternal torment in hell.
# Revelations and beliefs of Christianity (Chapter 48)
Holbach tries to distinguish between facts and religious myths; only after the historically oriented presentation of the previous chapters does the work deal with revelation. From the outset, the author endeavors to expose the deviancy of Christian beliefs, beginning with a mocking depiction of the Biblical creation myth: "As soon as this Adam has seen the light of the world, his Creator sets a trap for him.. ". Similarly absurd is the atoning sacrifice of Jesus Christ. Morality based on such an arbitrary God must be uncertain. The question of the extent to which the evil in the world is compatible with the alleged goodness of God (theodicy problem) cannot be answered by the existence of a devil or by the inexplicability of God's actions:
To have an idea of God, one could not turn to revelation, for it could not prove its own correctness. Doubts about their statements would not be brushed aside on the grounds that they are mysteries, for a benevolent God would express himself clearly to everyone. Obviously, this is not the case, since everyone interprets the Bible differently, including theologians. In fact, Christianity offers no advantage over any other "superstition that pollutes the universe", such as the belief in Brahma or Odin. There is no real evidence for miracles; they were invented to convince people of the impossible. The vague prophecies of the Old Testament were attempted to be fulfilled by forced interpretations and allegories. Martyrs would not prove anything either, because not only fanaticism but all emotions have their martyrs.
Holbach asks how such qualities as infinity, eternity, omnipotence, or justice are compatible with the God of the Bible. The Trinity could be established only by forceful explanations of the Scriptures; the dogmas of the Incarnation and the Resurrection had evidently been adopted by other religions. Not only is the idea of hell incompatible with a benevolent God but it also serves to subjugate people and to cloud their reason. Besides, it is not belief in heaven and hell that would keep people from rampant behavior, but good laws and a sound education. According to Holbach, angels are to the imagination of Christians what nymphs, larks, and fairies were to the imagination of pagans and Romans. Again, he emphasizes the parallels with other beliefs: Belief in Satan comes from earlier religions, Plato's concept of purgatory.
# Practice of Faith and Sacred Scripture (Chapters 9 and 10)
After discussing the central tenets of the Christian faith, Holbach briefly discusses the "childish and ridiculous ceremonies" of Christians. He said that baptism was a "mystery impenetrable to reason, the efficacy of which has been disproved by experience" because sins were apparently committed even after baptism. Even in the case of transubstantiation (the change of bread and wine into the body and blood of Jesus Christ), confession, prayer, and exorcism, "everything is a mystery, everything is magic, everything is incomprehensible". This is followed by a brief discussion of the contents of the sacred books. Unlike the Biblical exegesis advocated by some modern theologians, which interprets certain passages of Scripture as symbolic, Holbach took the Bible literally. The very beginning of the Bible reveals a 'deep ignorance of the laws of physics' and is full of contradictions. The whole of the Old Testament is a "clumsy collection of obscure and incoherent revelations". Holbach finds the New Testament hardly more credible and points to a number of places where the Gospels contradict each other. In view of such a book, it is not surprising that Christians repeatedly argued about what their God wanted them to do:
# Christian morals and virtues (Chapter 1113)
Holbach rejects the notion that without a supernatural revelation, no morality is possible. In fact, morality has always existed as a necessary part of society. The thinkers of pre-Christian societies  Socrates, Confucius, or the Gymnosophists  were no better than Jesus Christ and would refute the Christian claim to unique values such as justice, patriotism, patience, or gentleness. Far from sanctifying these values, Christianity only makes them insecure because a capricious God cannot possibly serve as a solid ethical basis. Since the idea of a cruel God has always impressed fanatics more deeply than that of a benevolent God, Christianity has been responsible for more bloodshed than any pagan superstition. Secular rulers would also have suffered from the self-willed moral views of the Christians. Instead of forbidding crime in the name of God, we should teach a 'natural morality' that points to man's self-preservation and his place in society.
Holbach describes the Christian virtues as being of little use to man. Love for an unjust and fearful God is hardly possible and, if followed, accompanied by zeal: "A true Christian must be enraged when sin is committed against God". It is in this context that the missions and the violence associated with them should also be understood. When soft-hearted persons felt romantic devotion to God, they viewed him only from a kindly standpoint, overlooking his unpleasant qualities. Neighborly love or love of one's enemies is unrealistic, for one can love another person only if one knows him and he contributes to one's own happiness. Faith had been elevated to a virtue only to prevent reason-based thinking and to maintain confidence in Christian officials. Blinded by the hope of eternal life, believers would lose sight of present happiness; the Catholic virtue of modesty demeans man and robs him of agency. Celibacy and the ban on divorce are criticized with similarly sharp anti-clericalism. On the whole, says Holbach, no true morality is compatible with the Christian religion:
Prayer is also absurd because it contradicts the claim of God's immutability; in other words, prayer presupposes a capricious God. Religious holidays caused urgent work to rest unnecessarily. Like few other cults, Christianity makes its adherents dependent on baptism, confession, and the threat of excommunication from the priesthood. Instead of educating a useful, enlightened citizen, from the very beginning people are being injected with a prejudice that always serves only the priests.
# Political and social influence of the clergy (Chapters 14 and 15)
After the reflections on Christian ethics, the political consequences of Christianity are examined. Holbach notes that in all Christian countries, two opposing legal systems arise, which fight each other; through the church, a state within the state arises. Because of the inevitable discord between the Christian denominations, between the Orthodox and the heretics, politics has always had to intervene. The Church has always sought to manipulate princes and rulers to its advantage. This leads to a tyranny under which the scientific, economic, cultural and social life of the state comes to a standstill. An enlightened and just ruler, on the other hand, who is serious about the welfare of his "subjects", has no need to promote superstition.
For Holbach, the Church's tyrannical claim to power is due to Christian doctrine, which is based on the infallible divine authority. In a historical overview, he goes on to explain that the wealth built up by the early bishops led to discord and power struggles among the clergy until the bishop of Rome finally ascended the throne and established a theocracy. Ultimately, he said, the Catholic religion was invented only to secure the power of the priesthood, and the Reformation, too, was a failed enterprise that could not rid itself of superstition. A Christian society is responsible for the evils that the priesthood inflicts upon it.
# Concluding word (Chapter 16)
The final word of Christianisme dévoilé is addressed mainly to the rulers, which was quite common for works of that time. Holbach makes it clear that it is in the interest of political officials to break away from the Christian religion and its clergy. His definition of religion from a political point of view resembles Marx's religious-critical theses:
It was the task of the enlightened ruler, not the church, to teach morality and to enforce justice. Even if Christianity does deter some people from committing crimes - which is doubtful - those benefits are nothing compared with the immense harm it has done. In contrast to Voltaire, who directed his educational program to the educated classes, Holbach called for a public education that included all people regardless of their origin.
With a quasi-religious appeal, Holbach optimistically concludes that the rulers have nothing to fear from an enlightened people, and that truth and reason will ultimately triumph. Although Holbach also puts his hopes ultimately on an enlightened monarch, he breaks away from Voltaire's plan to draw the rulers to the side of the Enlightenment through tactical maneuvers.
story_text_b:
In the mid-22nd century, violent and prolonged solar storms enlarge the Van Allen radiation belt, which deteriorated the ionosphere of the Earth. The solar radiation bombarding the planet increased surface temperatures, raised the levels of the seas, and so established a tropical climate throughout most of the planet; with most of Earth no longer habitable by humans, the survivors migrate to the North Pole and to the South Pole, which the planetary tropical climate has rendered fit for human habitation.
In 2145, under the command of Colonel Riggs, Dr Robert Kerans is part of a scientific expedition sent to catalogue the flora and fauna of the lagoon that covers the city of London. In the course of their scientific work, the members of the expedition begin to experience strange dreams. Amidst talk of the army and the scientists moving north, Lieutenant Hardman, the other officer in the expedition, flees the London lagoon and heads south; a search team sent to fetch him failed.
As the other inhabitants of the lagoon finally flee the overheating sunlight and head north, Kerans and two other scientists, the reclusive Dr. Beatrice Dahl and Dr Alan Bodkin, decided to remain. Moreover, a group of pirates, led by a man named Strangman, arrive to loot treasures from the deep waters of the London lagoon. After draining the lagoon, Strangman and his pirates expose the city of London, which disgusts the scientists Kerans and Bodkin; the latter attempts and fails to explode the flood defences and re-flood the London area. Afterwards, with Kerans and Beatrice resigned to their fate, the pirate leader Strangman vengefully pursues and kills the scientist Bodkin.
Meanwhile, Strangman and his pirates become suspicious of Kerans, and they imprison him and Dr. Dahl. The pirates torture Kerans, which he survives; although weakened by the torture, Kerans attempts and fails to free Dahl from captivity. Kerans and Dahl are confronted by Strangman and his pirates, but Colonel Riggs and the army return to rescue them from the pirates. Rather than punish Strangman, the military authorities co-operate with him, which angers and frustrates Dr. Kerans, who then successfully re-floods the lagoon, at which Dr. Bodkin had failed.
Weakened by a wound, Kerans flees the lagoon and heads southwards, without aim, and encounters the frail figure of Lieutenant Hardman, who has become blind. After aiding Hardman, Dr. Kerans continues travelling south, like “a second Adam searching for the forgotten paradises of the reborn sun.”

story_text_a:
Medical student Nelson Wright walks onto a beach one day and proclaims “today is a good day to die”. He later convinces four of his classmates—Joe Hurley, David Labraccio, Rachel Manus, and Randy Steckle—to help him discover what lies beyond death. Nelson flatlines for one minute before his classmates resuscitate him. While "dead", he experiences a sort of afterlife. He sees a vision of a boy he bullied as a child, Billy Mahoney. He merely tells his friends that he cannot describe what he saw, but something is there. The others follow Nelson's daring feat.
Joe flatlines next, and he experiences an erotic afterlife sequence linked to his sexually promiscuous lifestyle. He agrees with Nelson's claim that something indeed exists. After arguing with Rachel and out-bidding her on the length of time that they are willing to remain “dead”, David is third to flatline on Halloween, and he sees a vision of a girl, Winnie Hicks, whom he bullied in grade school. The three men start to experience hallucinations related to their afterlife visions. Nelson gets physically assaulted by Billy Mahoney twice. Joe, engaged to be married, is haunted by the women that he surreptitiously videotaped during his sexual dalliances, the women taunting Joe with the same come-ons, lines and false promises he used on them. David is confronted by the 8-year-old Winnie Hicks on a train, and she verbally taunts him the way he taunted her.
Rachel decides to flatline next. David rushes in, intending to stop the others from giving Rachel their same fate, but she is already "dead" when he arrives. Rachel nearly dies permanently when the power goes out and the men are unable to shock her with the defibrillator paddles. She survives, but she too is haunted by the memory of her father committing suicide when she was young.
The three men finally reveal their harrowing experiences to one another, and David decides to put his visions to a stop. Meanwhile, Joe's fiancée, Anne, comes to his apartment and, having discovered his collection of videos, ends their relationship. Joe's visions cease after Anne leaves him.
David goes to visit a now adult Winnie Hicks and apologizes to her. Winnie accepts his apology and thanks him. David immediately feels a weight lifted off his shoulders. David then finds Nelson, who accompanied David to visit Winnie, beating himself with a climbing axe. In Nelson's mind, however, Billy is again attempting to beat him to death. David stops him, and they return to town, where Rachel confronts Nelson about withholding the supernatural nature of the experiments from the rest of them, then storms off. David later instructs Joe and Randy to help Nelson find Billy and that under no uncertain terms is Nelson to be left alone.
Having an idea of what Rachel has experienced, David offers to let Rachel stay with him and they go to bed together. While Rachel and David are together, Nelson takes Randy and Joe to a graveyard. He reveals that he killed Billy as a kid by throwing rocks at him until he fell out of a tree. The two try to tell Nelson that what he did was not intentional, but Nelson makes a cryptic choice about making amends. Confused and worried, they attempt to clarify, but are stranded when Nelson in his furor storms off in Joe's Mustang.
David leaves Rachel alone in order to rescue Joe and Randy at the cemetery. While alone, Rachel goes to the bathroom and finds her father. He apologizes to his daughter and her guilt over his death is lifted when she discovers that he was addicted to morphine and that his suicide was related to post-traumatic stress disorder stemming from his service in the Vietnam War. Nelson calls David's house, and when Rachel answers he tells her that he needs to flatline again in order to make amends. He apologizes for involving her and their friends in his reckless plan. Rachel tries to tell Nelson that it does not matter, but Nelson counters with the belief that everything that they say and do matters.
The three men realize to their shock what he intends and race to stop Nelson, who has been dead for an estimated nine minutes already. Rachel soon finds them, and the four friends work feverishly to save Nelson. In the afterlife, Nelson is experiencing himself as a young boy being stoned by Billy from the tree. Nelson dies in the afterlife from the fall, and his friends cannot revive him. When all of them except David are about to give up, Billy forgives Nelson, and David gives Nelson one last shock. This brings him back, and Nelson tells them, "It wasn't such a good day to die."
story_text_b: Ravi Yadav (Vinod Khanna) is the servant of Manohar Singh (Rajiv Verma). He has a younger brother, Rohan Yadav (Salman Khan). When Ravi is falsely accused of killing a woman, and sentenced to 12 years in prison, Manohar Singh's wife Renuka (Moushumi Chatterjee) assures him that she will take care of Rohan.

story_text_a:
The story takes place in Paris at the end of the 19th century. In Simone Pistache's Café "Le bal du paradis" at the Montmartre, dancers entertain their audience with the cancan. Actually, this dance is considered immoral and is therefore forbidden; but Judge Paul Barriere, chairman of the police committee, likes to turn a blind eye because he himself appreciates the cancan. One day, however, the judge is assigned a new colleague, young Philippe Forrestier, to whom this dance is a thorn in the eye. As soon as he takes office, he also sends some policemen to the "notorious" place, and as soon as the dancers are on the stage, they are also arrested. Philippe's boss and his friend, the lawyer François Durnais, narrowly escape arrest, because it also threatens the guests of the establishment.
To Forestier's chagrin, there are no witnesses claiming to have seen immorality at the Cancan. So he tries again the very next night  and this time he has photographers in tow to capture the scandal in the picture. He himself mingles unnoticed among the guests and involves Simone in a conversation. In the process, he learns that his troupe was able to dance undisturbed today because the police had been bribed. Simone's colleague Claudine can barely keep her boss from revealing her source to the curious. Immediately, the police interrupt the dance and arrest the girls a second time.
Little by little, Simone and Philippe Forrestier begin to like each other. Paul and François, who is also in love with Simone, are determined to prevent their romance from turning into a marriage. So during a ball of the best Parisian society, they create a sinister situation in which Philippe must realize that a connection with Simone would mean the end of his career in the police service. So he breaks off his relationship with her.
The "Bal du Paradis" is to host a great celebration for the artists of Paris. In order to finance the ball, Simone received a loan from her admirer François. During the preparations, the two get a little closer again. Eventually, Simone also reconciles with Philippe, who suddenly does not want to leave her. In order to take out François, who is actually more important to her, because he does not want to marry her, Simone proceeds with a ruse: as a guarantee for the financing of the ball, she has transferred her restaurant to him, and then when after some time the girls start dancing their cancan, François is arrested as a business owner.
Francois is charged. Paul Barriere is testifying in his favor. The trial ends with an acquittal. However, the "League Against Immorality" is not satisfied with this. That's why Philippe's arranging a local appointment. The eyewitnesses need to realize that the dancing itself is not immoral because it does not promote fornication. Suddenly, police officers approach Simone and take her to the car that usually transports prisoners to the prison. But there's only François, who she knows loves her; he's been waiting for her.
story_text_b:
One day in this mall where we follow a group of very different people with varied needs, who will be seriously affected when a man enters with the intention of killing everyone in his path. Abuse, excess, lack of control, humiliation, loss and feeling absurd will be things to be dealt with here.
The development starts out promising, but they don't delve too deeply into the little stories that they're going to give us, except for very few exceptions.
The pursuit of punishment, the adolescent love, the sense of justice, which might rather be the sense of justifying a humiliation, at least as far as the man accused of perverse behavior, and this young man with a different way of thinking, who would discover several things on this day that would help him change some of his thoughts.

story_text_a:
Undercover cop Muscles (Jackie Chan) enlists his childhood friends, the "Five Lucky Stars", to travel to Japan to help him catch a Yakuza group.
A corrupt Hong Kong cop (Lam Ching Ying) flees to Tokyo to join his fellow mobsters, whose headquarters are secretly built under an amusement park (filmed in Fuji-Q Highland). Two loyal cops, Ricky (Yuen Biao) and Muscle (Jackie Chan), travel there to apprehend him and uncover the mobsters’ lair, but Ricky is kidnapped in a fight. Muscle goes into hiding and calls his supervisor to send help; since the mobsters already have information on the officers of the Hong Kong Royal Police Force, Muscle asks to send his orphanage friends, nicknamed the Five Lucky Stars, over to assist. The supervisor agrees and collects the five friends, who are all either petty criminals or low-wage workers. They refuse to aid the police, but the supervisor cunningly sets up a false story in the media that accuses the five of robbing a bank of millions of dollars, blackmailing them into helping. They ultimately agree when the supervisor teams them up with a rookie policewoman, Swordflower, who becomes an object of lustful target to the five. They travel to Tokyo and that night, Kidstuff (Sammo Hung), the Stars' most rational and talented member, and Swordflower go to Muscle’s apartment. After defeating some thugs, Muscle reunites with Kidstuff. The operation is to send phony money to the mobsters to allow the five to enter their lair, and that way they can get closer to freeing Ricky and apprehending the criminals. After a prolonged battle at the bowels of the amusement park, the criminals lose and the Lucky Stars receive a place to live back at Hong Kong as their reward.
story_text_b: Two officers, Muscle and Ricky, are investigating a case of stolen jewelry. Their investigation leads them to Japan where Ricky is captured by the Ninja Gang. Muscle then has to ask for help from his former colleagues at the orphanage...

story_text_a:
Arvind (Vivek Oberoi) and Lakshmi (Antara Mali) are in love and want to get married. However, Lakshmi's dad, a cop, is against their affair. Hence the two decide to elope from Delhi and travel to get married at Arvind's ancestral haveli in Rajgarh, Alwar, Rajasthan, by road, passing by a desert, in a Tata Safari.
After an escape from an aggravated assault by a mad wayfarer, they bump into a smooth-talking hitchhiker Babu (Manoj Bajpayee), who is stranded in the middle of nowhere. Babu convinces the young couple to give him a lift. Travelling with Babu proves a nightmare for Arvind and Lakshmi as Babu turns out to be a psychopath. Soon, Lakshmi finds herself as hostage of an armed Babu. Thanks to the timely intervention of a truck driver Inderpal (Makrand Deshpande) and the highway petrol bunk owner, an aspiring actor Bhanwar Singh (Rajpal Yadav), Arvind rescues Lakshmi from Babu.
After a while, Babu again finds a way, after attacking Inderpal, and again attacks the couple by haunting them on the road via Inderpal's truck. But, this time, Babu fails to get hold of the couple. After lodging an FIR, in the nearest police station, the couple finds a motel and they  recuperate. The next day Babu again attacks the couple and elopes with Lakshmi.
When the car breaks down on the way, Babu kills another victim, a traveler (Snehal Dabi) attracted to Lakshmi, and elopes in the traveler's vehicle. As the cops are on their way to catch hold of him, he manages to evade them.
On the other hand, the cops suspect Arvind as the serial killer, as he first eloped with Lakshmi, who is D.C.P's daughter. This irresponsible intervention of the cop (Sayaji Shinde), who fail to trust Arvind, makes it impossible to chase Lakshmi. Finally, a frustrated Arvind, manages to escape with the cops' jeep. The full focus of the police is now on Arvind as they believe him to have committed a murder and dumped the body in a car and that the story of Babu and Lakshmi is a fabrication. Arvind manages to flee to a small bar where he reunites with Inderpal. He and Inderpal now try to track Babu down with the help of Inderpal's truck but are spotted by the police who give a chase. Inderpal is injured in the gunfight and Arvind drives him to a hospital.
Meanwhile, Babu forces his way into a bungalow by attacking its caretaker while the owner was away. There, Lakshmi begins to show signs that she is on Babu's side. The caretaker of the house is tied up but manages to call the police on Babu. At the same time, the police also find Arvind's vehicle and in it, a photograph of himself and Lakshmi, indicating that Arvind is innocent and was telling the truth. At the hospital, Arvind has an encounter with the police and overcomes a cop and is about to tie him up when that cop gets informed through the radio that Arvind is innocent.
The police reach the bungalow the following morning where Babu kills two policemen before escaping. Arvind, finally having his name cleared, joins the police in chasing down Babu. He takes control of a police bike after its rider was shot down by Babu. Arvind chases Babu into the desert where the vehicle breaks down again. Babu and Lakshmi get out of the car and Arvind too gets off his bike and starts coming for Babu. Babu tells Lakshmi that there is only one bullet left in the gun and that will kill Arvind. However, just as he is about to shoot, Lakshmi attacks Babu, causing the last bullet to miss. Arvind takes advantage of the distraction and attacks Babu. Arvind badly beats Babu and the couple, reunited, leave Babu to die in the desert and continue on their journey on the police bike.
story_text_b:
Arvind and Lakshmi love each other and want to get married, but Lakshmi's father is against this relationship. So the two set off for Jodhpur, Rajasthan, to secretly get engaged.
On the way, they encounter a man whose car was supposedly stopped on the road. Since they don't want to leave him in the middle of the desert, they take him with them. This man, Babu, is about to go down on them and turn out to be a psychopath. When the two want to get rid of him, Babu threatens Arvind with a gun, so Arvind is forced to let Lakshmi and Babu travel on their own.
Only after a long back and forth can Arvind, with the help of a truck driver, rescue Lakshmi from Babu's violence after a chase. Arvind shoots Babu and leaves him lying in the desert while the two can finally continue their journey.

story_text_a:
One year after the events of Agent 007 - Live and Let Die, James Bond discovers that he is the next target of Francisco Scaramanga, one of the world's top assassins who is known to kill his victims with golden bullets detonated from a gun that can also be made of gold. M then relieves Bond of his mission, which involves a new solar-powered machine that scientist Gibson wants to use to solve the energy crisis, and tells him that he has to find the killer under the counter.
007 discovers, thanks to Q, that Scaramanga's supplier is a man named Lazar, an artisan who builds custom-made weapons in Macau, where he travels and meets Scaramanga's charming lover Andrea Anders in Hong Kong. Gibson is robbed of an essential component by Nick Nack, the killer's dwarf butler, and the scientist himself is killed.
Bond then continues his investigation with the support of Police Lieutenant Hip, who brings him to M and Q, who instruct him to retrieve the component and kill Scaramanga, and Andrea herself, whom he manages to seduce.
After several twists and turns, Bond finally arrives on the island where Scaramanga lives in a beautiful mansion powered by solar technology that the killer intends to sell to the highest bidder. After a mushroom-based lunch prepared by Nick Nack, the two are challenged to a duel in the hall of mirrors of the estate and Bond finally succeeds in killing Scaramanga and destroying his dwelling. Eventually defeating Nick Nack's last tailspin, James manages to return to England with his co-worker Mary Goodnight, who has always been in love with him.
story_text_b:
Brief synopsis of the film
The plot has Bond being sent after the Solex Stirrer, a device that can harness the energy of the sun, for which he must confront assassin Francisco Scaramanga, "the man with the golden gun". The action culminates in a duel in which the fate of the Solex is clarified.
Full synopsis
In the pre-credits sequence, the murderer Francisco Scaramanga (Christopher Lee) leads a pleasant life on a paradise island with his partner Andrea Anders (Maud Adams). Unbeknownst to him, his servant Nick Nack (Hervé Villechaize), pays a gangster named Rodney (Marc Lawrence) to duel with Scaramanga and, tricked by Nick Nack, the killer falls into a house of laughter, also shooting range where replicas of a cowboy and Al Capone appear. In a quick maneuver, Scaramanga kills the gangster and shoots at a replica of 007.
A golden bullet with the number 007 engraved on it arrives at MI6 Headquarters. This means that the killer wants to liquidate 007 (Roger Moore). He tells M (Bernard Lee) what little he knows about Scaramanga in the presence of Bill Tanner (Michael Goodliffe) and Colthorpe (James Cossins), the son of a Cuban circus director and an English knife thrower and expert marksman at the age of 10, temporarily hired by the KGB and later a professional assassin who charges a million dollars for killing, his only characteristic feature a third nipple. M worried about his agent asks him to go into hiding even though Bond was on a mission to find Gibson, a renowned scientist who would help solve the energy crisis. Bond on his way out asks for information from Moneypenny who tells him that his partner Bill Fairbanks 002 would probably have been killed by a Scaramanga bullet in a cabaret.
Bond visits the cabaret in Beirut where he observes a beautiful woman named Saida (Carmen du Sautoy) characterized by a strange amulet in her navel, Bond visits her in her dressing room where he tells her that she had a relationship with 002 and the bullet fired had ended her life but the bullet went through her neck hitting the wall almost crushing, so the bullet became the amulet in Saida's navel. When Bond seduces her to remove the bullet, several bullies attack Bond and he manages to neutralize them and in the confusion manages to steal the "amulet". Bond heads to Q's (Desmond Llewelyn) laboratory where he and his assistant Colthorpe discover that the bullet was made by a rarely known gunsmith named Lazar who lives in Macau. Bond travels there where he interrogates Lazar (Marne Maitland) who denies knowing Scaramanga personally but says he sells the bullets to a stranger in the casino. Later in the casino, Lazar leaves the bullets while Andrea collects them while sending the money, Bond watches her and follows her to Hong Kong and meets an MI6 agent named Mary Goodnight (Britt Ekland). The two follow the woman to the Peninsula Hotel and Bond observes Andrea in the shower of the room, she with her gun threatens the agent but 007 controls the situation and forcibly interrogates her, she tells him that Scaramanga goes to a strip club called Bottoms Up and owned a white suit with a black tie. That night Bond watches the place and when he notices that Scaramanga did not show up he decides to go to the club without knowing that the killer was on a roof and, shooting Gibson (Gordon Everett), Bond tries to look for Scaramanga but is stopped by Lieutenant Hip (Soon-Taik Oh) and, seeing that he is not taken to the police station, Bond escapes on the wrecked RMS Queen Elizabeth and discovers there a small MI6 barracks where M, Q and Frazier (Gerald James) are waiting for him, Hip presents himself as an MI6 contact in Hong Kong and M informs Bond that Scaramanga may be related to Hai, a Thai businessman who probably would have paid a million dollars to kill Gibson, the inventor of the Agitator Solex, a device capable of converting sunlight into energy, designed to end the hydrocarbon crisis. Before he died, Gibson had shown it to Hip, but Hip discovers that the Solex wasn't on the body. Bond, to infiltrate and extract information, asks Q for a third artificial nipple so he can supplant Scaramanga.
Bond travels to Bangkok, Thailand with Hip and manages to break into Hai Fat's house posing as Scaramanga and when he is tempted to swim with a beautiful woman named Chew Mee (Francoise Therry) is stopped by Hai Fat (Richard Loo), who believes Bond is Scaramanga. For his part, Bond continues to pretend to be him by showing the fake third nipple, and warns him that MI6 is involved in tracking down the Solex and asks for a million more for "killing Bond". Hai Fat decides to think it over and invites Bond to dinner and afterwards Bond leaves the property not knowing that the real Scaramanga was hiding in Hai Fat's office and watching him. Bond accepts Hai Fat's invitation and leaves accompanied by Hip and his nieces Nara (Qiu Yuen) and Cha (Joie Vejjajiva), but upon entering Hai Fat's house he is captured by Nick Nack and two sumo wrestlers and when the former intends to kill him, Hai Fat orders that he be left alive for the time being. The next day Bond wakes up at a martial arts school, where he first observes a sword fight to the death and then confronts two students including Chula (Chan Yiu Lam). After a difficult fight Bond defeats him and flees, being helped by Hip and his nieces who were also fighting against the other students, but upon seeing Chula and other karatecas with black belts they flee. Chula and the other students follow Bond to a nearby river, where the agent uses a sampan to escape, but failing causes a child to operate it to escape Chula at high speed, passing among several tourists in Thailand, among whom was Sheriff J. W. Pepper (Clifton James) and his wife. When Chula and the others thought they'd lost Bond, he sank the students' boat and escaped.
Hai Fat, on the other hand, learns that Bond has escaped and warns Scaramanga to go into hiding, but Scaramanga covertly fires his gun and kills Hai Fat and takes control of his businesses. Also, the villain gets the Solex Stirrer after the businessman before he died asked him to hide it too. That night Goodnight and Bond have dinner and intend to spend the night together, but are interrupted by Anders. Bond hides Goodnight, and Anders confesses to Bond that he sent the bullet with his number engraved on it to free her from Scaramanga's yoke, and Bond proposes that he get him the Solex Stirrer in exchange for his freedom and Scaramanga's death. Bond and Anders spend the night together with Goodnight hiding in the closet. As Anders returns to Scaramanga's reed, Goodnight comes out of the closet and criticizes Bond for accepting the Solex deal with Anders. The next day Bond meets Anders at a boxing stadium to hand him the Solex, but discovers that she had been killed by Scaramanga, and he interviews Bond while Nick Nack was threatening him with a gun and telling him about his passion for killing, after he had killed the tamer who had injured his own elephant as a child. Bond pretending to buy peanuts finds the Solex on the floor and gives it to Hip disguised as a salesman and this gives it to Goodnight. Hip asks her to call the police, while she had followed Nick Nack from the Bottoms Up club after recognizing him. Goodnight in turn follows Nick Nack, writes down the license plate of Scaramanga's car and places a tracking device on him, but is kidnapped and locked in the trunk by him. With the Solex in her possession, Goodnight uses the transponder to alert Bond and Hip of her abduction, but they can no longer use their car because she has the keys. Accordingly, Bond heads to a nearby dealership and seizes a car that Sheriff Pepper was viewing inside. He recognizes Bond and the two pursue Scaramanga's car, only to be pursued by the police. Bond and Pepper manage to follow Scaramanga to a small stable, where the Sheriff is stopped by the police while Bond and the police observe that Scaramanga had turned his car into a small plane to escape. Bond informs M that Scaramanga had escaped with Goodnight and the Solex. But the car-plane had been located by the transceiver, and soon a sailor informed them that Goodnight's signal had been intercepted from a small island near China.
007 travels by seaplane to Ko Tapu, the lair of Scaramanga, who gives orders to the Chinese vigilantes so that Bond can enter the island. Scaramanga lives with an agreement with China, and shows Bond his luxurious life and especially the section of electricity obtained from the solar power maintained by Kra (Sonny Caldinez). Scaramanga shows Bond the Solex Stirrer, which he has used to design a prototype weapon with which he destroys Bond's seaplane. Scaramanga tells Bond that he will later sell the Solex to the highest bidder, whom he would help to have a power plant just like his. Scaramanga, Bond and Goodnight have lunch, and Scaramanga compares himself to Bond, but Bond denies the comparison and the killer proposes to the agent a duel: his gold pistol versus Bond's Walther PPK. At the start of the duel Scaramanga disappears and Bond sets out to find him, but first he convinces Nick Nack that all that would belong to him (Nick Nack) if Scaramanga died. He guides Bond first to the gym and then to the shooting range, where the mannequins of a cowboy and Al Capone are located. Bond sneaks into the compound bypassing security cameras, being pursued by Scaramanga. Bond tricks Scaramanga with his replica and kills him with a shot, while Goodnight at the power plant hits Kra causing him to fall into one of the tanks of liquid helium that must be at low temperature to not explode, and in a dangerous situation Bond retrieves the Solex and together with Goodnight escape from the island, which eventually explodes. Then, in Scaramanga's reed, Nick Nack tries to kill Bond, but fails, and Bond captures him by leaving him in the back of the boat. Next Bond and Goodnight have their romantic moment in Scaramanga's reed, ignoring a call from M.

story_text_a: During a stormy night, a giant billboard falls on the wall of a barrio cerrado in Mexico City. Three young thieves from the slums break into the closed and privately guarded wealthy settlement La zona and kill an elderly woman whom they discover during her break-in. As a result, the angry residents of the wealthy neighborhood themselves take up the pursuit of the perpetrators and thus also come into conflict with the police.
story_text_b: Three teenagers from Mexico City break into a house, but the robbery goes wrong and they kill the old woman who lives there, while a guard is shot by mistake. Rather than notify the authorities, which would result in the closure of the residence, the residents decide to take justice into their own hands. A ruthless manhunt begins, while outside a policeman conducts the investigation.

story_text_a:
As Mother's Day approaches, a group of seemingly disconnected people in Atlanta embrace the relationship with their mothers.
Sandy is a divorced mother of two sons, Mikey and Peter, whose ex-husband, Henry, has recently remarried a woman, Tina. Still getting used to this, she meets Bradley, a former Marine, at the grocery store. Bradley's wife, Dana, a Navy lieutenant, died a year ago, leaving him with their two daughters, Vicky and Rachel. Everyone misses her terribly.
Kristin, adopted from birth, has a daughter of her own, Katie, and is considering marrying her daughter's father, Zack. She considers her life incomplete and her friend Jesse encourages her to find her birth mother. Jesse also happens to be Sandy's best friend.
Jesse and his sister Gabi have their own problems with their parents, whom they consider too racist and homophobic to be in their lives: Jesse is married and has a son, Tanner with Russell, a doctor originally from India. Gabi is married to her girlfriend Max and has a son, Charlie. When your parents, Earl and Florence, suddenly appear, it's necessary to catch up.
While in Atlanta promoting her latest book, Miranda, an accomplished author and television personality, receives a surprise visit from Kristin, her daughter, whom she was forced to give up for adoption at birth. Their reconciliation leads Kristin to ask Zach to marry her on the air and get married on the same day, so that Miranda can participate.
Jesse and Gabi's parents ambush them and their partners in their RV and, with the help of Russell's mother via Skype, force him to reconcile with Jesse. Later, the families, including their mother, who flies in from Las Vegas, celebrate Mother's Day with a picnic in the park.
Sandy and Bradley meet again by chance in the hospital. She's there because of her son's asthma attack, he's there because of a mishap at the Mother's Day party he was throwing that landed him in the hospital with a broken leg. By helping her out of a vending machine, combined with encouragement from his daughters, Bradley finally begins to see her in a positive light.
story_text_b:
On a very stormy night, Elyne Mitchell tells her daughter Indi the story of the silver stallion Thowra.
He was born on just such a stormy night, and since the Aborigines call the wind that blows over the highlands of Australia Thowra, this young horse should bear that name as well. His mother passed on all her knowledge to him so that he could survive in the wilderness. It wasn't long before he encountered the greatest threat to them: man. He was almost caught, but thanks to the intervention of his mother Berga, he escaped the danger. Quickly, however, he moved on to the next: he came too close to Brolga, the lead shepherd of another flock. Thowra and his mother were pursued by the angry stallion until they reached their territory and Thowra's father, Yarraman, was able to drive away the strange stallion.
However, as the people spread throughout the land, they began hunting wild horses and the young stallions with the peculiar color. One of the men was Cody, who had almost caught the stallion as a foal. Now that Thowra had grown into a stately and powerful stallion, the man chased him in vain. Each time he escaped, but he had to watch as Brolga challenged his father Yarraman and defeated him in battle. So Brolga took over the herd and Thowra started a small family of his own. Taking advantage of this, Cody bought a young golden mare at an auction to lure and capture the silver stallion. But Thowra kidnapped the mare without Cody being able to do anything about it. Over the year, she got a foal from Thowra and after Cody managed to capture both the mare and the foal, the silver stallion freed the two again.
Meanwhile, Brolga also claimed Thowra's small herd. In a fierce battle, the silver stallion proved that he is the heir and rightful king of the wild.
Parallel to the story Elyne Mitchell tells her daughter, she writes it down and experiences adventures with the girl herself in the Australian Highlands. One day, Indi Mitchell is forced to witness Jock's brutal attempts to tame wild horses. Indi is horrified, since her mother had taught her to treat nature and its creatures with respect. During a conversation between Jock and her mother, which Indi overhears by chance, she realizes that the story of the silver stallion does not seem to be a legend, but true, because Jock's assistant Egan reports about his just unsuccessful hunt for a wild horse. According to him, this ghostly horse ended up jumping off the cliffs in its escape, which it could not have survived. However, as Indi and her mother feel the wind of the highlands blowing in their faces outside their house in the evening, this ghost horse has only seemingly sacrificed itself. They are confident that future generations will continue to tell the story of a mighty silver Mustang, a ghost horse that appears and disappears in the highlands, but no one will know where Berga's son wandered.

story_text_a:
The novel portrays the fictional, world-dominant platform company Circle, which has not only surpassed Facebook, Twitter, and Google, but also the equally fictional companies Alacrity, Zoopa, Jefe, and Quan, and their combined offerings.
Maebelline Mae Holland, a college graduate, begins her new job at The Circle, a powerful IT company run by the so-called "Three Wise Men". Mae owes her employment to her best friend and former college roommate, Annie, who is also one of the 40 most influential people in the company. Mae starts at Customer Experience, the company's customer service department, but quickly rises through the company's hierarchy. From the beginning, Mae is impressed by the Circle's amenities, such as access to world-class technology, private residences, gyms, other recreational facilities, and parties. Ma's first day at the Circle ends with a party where she meets Francis, with whom she becomes romantically involved. Later, Mae meets a mysterious co-worker named "Kalden" and is also drawn to him, though she fails to learn his status at the company or even his last name.
In the meantime, the Circle continues to develop a number of advanced technologies, including 'SeeChange': lightweight, portable cameras that transmit real-time video to any location with minimal effort. The 'SeeChange' cameras are worn around the clock by politicians, among others, who want to be 'transparent' and thus allow the public to see what they are doing at all times.
Mae's father is diagnosed with multiple sclerosis. Due to this illness, Mae enrolled her parents in her own health insurance with her employer The Circle, who in turn outfitted Mae's apartment with SeeChange cameras. After a brief encounter with the police, Mae finally agrees to wear a SeeChange body-worn camera and become "transparent". In doing so, she embodies her increasingly important role in the company, which is also symbolized by a public speech in which she makes the statements "Secrets are lies", "Sharing is healing" and "All private is theft". Her job now consists largely of walking around the company campus as an 'ambassador' and showing customers future products. Any hints that she herself has doubts about (lack of) privacy are now diminishing, unlike her former friend Mercer, who eventually insists on "disappearing from the map" to escape the ever-growing and far-reaching influence of the Circle and its technologies. Kalden contacts Mae and warns her that the Circle must be stopped, but she refuses to follow through on that thought.
Meanwhile, Annie becomes jealous of Mae's success and volunteers to become the first test subject for "PastPerfect" to cement her status within the company. "PastPerfect" compiles a complete family history of any person, using all the information available online. As part of this process, disturbing matters involving Annie's family also come to light. Eventually, the psychological strain on Annie from these revelations becomes so great that she falls into a coma. Exposed both by her parents' distrust of SeeChange's surveillance of her apartment and by the behavior of her ex-boyfriend Mercer  each through Mae's body camera publicly visible to her millions of followers, Mae becomes increasingly upset. When she demonstrates live a new program that can capture fugitive criminals in minutes, she also uses it to find Mercer. He tries to escape the video surveillance and commits suicide by deliberately falling from a bridge, meanwhile being pursued by drones and having no chance to "escape". Although initially depressed by this, Mae soon tries to negotiate away her depression over Mercer's death with the help of the charismatic "Wise Man" Eamon Bailey. So she concludes that he was a very depressed, antisocial person who refused to accept help from the community, and compares his actions to those of a person who commits suicide by jumping out of a window the moment the doctor arrives for a visit.
Kalden turns out to be the elusive "Wise Man" Ty Gospodinov, the original inventor and founder of the Circle. Mae agrees to meet with him in secret, and he tells her of his concern that a totalitarian regime will soon emerge, like a "surveillance society", unless something is done about it. He lays out the need for privacy in a digital age and asks them to help him break the circle because he can't do it alone. Mae thinks Ty is crazy, but pretends to support him  but then betrays him by telling the other founders of the Circle what happened. These will ensure that Ty is silenced. The book ends with Mae looking at Annie in the hospital and wondering when the time will come when people's thoughts will be made visible and for the public good, as the world has a right to do.
story_text_b:
When Mae Holland gets hired by the Circle, she doesn't look back. Based on a campus in California, Circle, an Internet service provider, connects personal emails, social networks, consumer purchases and banking transactions to a universal operating system, creating a new hyper-digital era of civility and transparency.
As the young woman walks around the circular headquarters, the open spaces, the huge glass cafeterias, the comfortable dormitories for those who stay to work in the evening (in La Colonie), the modernity of the premises and the intense activity delight her. There's all-night parties, famous musicians play on the lawn, sports activities, clubs and brunches are offered, and there's even an aquarium containing rare fish reported by the CEO.
Mae can't believe her chance to work for the most influential company there is - even if the campus absorbs her completely (several screens, several connected bracelets), distancing her more and more from her loved ones, even if she exposes herself to the eyes of the world by participating in the Circle's latest project, a technological advance as considerable as it is disturbing, total and live transparency.

story_text_a:
The young fighter Endel Nelis hides from Stalin's secret police (MGB) on the Estonian coast in Haapsalu in the early 1950s. Under the guise of a false identity, he gets a job as a gym teacher. He teaches the students fencing. Many of the young people are traumatized by the war and fatherless, and so Endel becomes a compensating father figure for them.
However, the school principal is suspicious of him because he considers fencing to be a "feudal" sport that does not belong in a workers' and peasants' state. However, at a parent meeting, the grandfather of the student Jaan strongly advocates that Endel Nelis be allowed to continue fencing lessons, and draws, much to the displeasure of the school principal, the other attendees to his side. As a result, the school principal has Endel's CV investigated by the secret police, and it turns out that he was a Wehrmacht soldier for a short time during the German occupation at the age of 18. Therefore, he had to fear being executed as a "traitor to the fatherland" and "enemy of the state" or being sent to the Gulag. Therefore, he had dropped his family name "Keller" and adopted his mother's birth name as a cover.
When his fencing class learns of a tournament in Leningrad, Endel must decide if he wants to take the risk of being arrested if he participates in it. Against the advice of his colleague Kadri, with whom he has fallen in love, he decides that the school team of four students will participate. Despite his team's success in the final, he is arrested and deported. Shortly thereafter, Stalin dies. Many prisoners are subsequently released from the camps, including Endel Nelis, whom Kadri awaits on the train platform in Haapsalu upon his return, but not Jaan's grandfather, who was also deported.
story_text_b:
Introductory screens set the background of the film: during World War II, Estonia was occupied by Nazi Germany, which recruited most of the men in the German army, and then was occupied by the Soviet Union, which considered German army soldiers to be criminals. After the war, the Soviets incorporated Estonia into the USSR.
A young man, Endel Nelis, arrives in Haapsalu, Soviet Socialist Republic of Estonia (then part of the Soviet Union) in the early 1950s, having left Leningrad to escape the secret police. He found work as a teacher and founded a sports club for his students, where he began to teach them his great passion: fencing. Displeased, the school principal begins to investigate Endel's background. Meanwhile, Endel's friend (and coach) Aleksei warns him not to return to Leningrad under any circumstances.
Fencing becomes a form of self-expression for the children, and Endel becomes a role model and a father figure. Learn to love children, many of whom have been orphaned. When the children want to participate in a national fencing tournament in Leningrad, Endel must make a choice; risk everything to bring the children to Leningrad or put their safety first and disappoint them.

story_text_a:
The three New York City yuppies Corey, Emily and David are on their way home from a company party. A stop at an ATM is said to have unintended consequences. From the service room, they're watching a brutal murder. But the killer has no intention of leaving the scene. He waits in the adjacent parking lot, his eyes fixed on the group. He strikes down a guard, as he did his previous victim, a passerby who was just walking his dog. In a panic, David rushes to the ATM, hoping to set off an alarm.
Then the perpetrator enters the room unexpectedly. Corey and David rush him, beat him up, and finally strangle him with a chain. That's not the end of the threat, I'm afraid. The intruder only resembled the perpetrator to create confusion. The mysterious perpetrator is still prowling around the building. Corey won't be able to hold it in the machine room after this shock. He runs across the parking lot, trips and falls. The killer seizes the opportunity and slowly and painfully strangles Corey on the floor. David ventures out of the hallway and drags Corey back to the machine room, the seriously injured one showing the last signs of life.
Time and time again, the killer makes his way to the back of the vending machine. But instead of breaking through the wall, water suddenly flows through the ventilation shaft - threatening to drown the three. Quickly, David and Emily collect all the outstanding booklets and set them on fire in a metal trash can to start the sprinkler system. But since David can't reach the sprinkler system's sensor on his own, Emily climbs on his shoulder. It automatically sends a distress call to the security authorities. When they finally trigger the device, David slips and falls over, with Emily hitting her head on a flyer and lying motionless in the water. Now only David is conscious. The killer drives the guard's car into David's car, which is then pushed into the machine room.
The police arrive and take him into custody. His clues to the real culprit and his countermeasure are ignored.
In the epilogue, the viewer sees the perpetrator studying location plans at a drawing table in preparation for the next, similar crime.
story_text_b: Kate works in advertising, but her boss refuses her a promotion because he does not find her stable enough, given that she is still single and has few connections in the company. She meets Nick at a wedding and their relationship begins to solidify when she attracts the attention of a co-worker who has always been interested in her.

story_text_a:
Following the end of World War II in Europe and the liberation of Denmark from German occupation in May 1945, the Wehrmacht and SS occupiers became prisoners of war. Returning to the Danish Army after service in the British Parachute Regiment, sergeant Carl Leopold Rasmussen furiously beats up a German prisoner for carrying a Danish flag. A group of young German prisoners are handed over to Rasmussen's commanding officer Captain Ebbe Jensen and sent to the west coast, where they are trained to use their bare hands to remove the mines that the Germans had buried in the sand.  They are warned not to expect any sympathy from the Danes, who resent their former occupiers. Rasmussen shares this contempt and is determined to treat the young prisoners without sympathy.
Rasmussen is rude to and contemptuous of them and the neighbouring farm treats them with hostility. After marching his squad onto the dunes, he promises that they will return home in three months, if they can each defuse six mines per hour for a total of 45,000 mines. Rasmussen's hostility begins to recede slightly and the boys' leader Sebastian Schumann attempts to remain optimistic as they discuss their plans for when they return home. The POWs are not given food due to post-war shortages and begin to suffer from malnourishment, with Ernst befriending a young local girl to steal some bread from her. The optimistic Wilhelm's arms are blown off and he dies in a field hospital. Most of the boys are poisoned by rat faeces in grain that they find on a nearby farm; they are treated by Rasmussen who makes them purge themselves with seawater.
Rasmussen begins to treat his charges more kindly, stealing food from the base for them and tries to maintain morale by reporting that Wilhelm has survived. He also allows the boys to use a device invented by Sebastian to improve productivity. Hearing rumours of Rasmussen stealing food for the boys, Ebbe brings a group of British soldiers to abuse and torment the boys. Rasmussen stops them but is confronted about the theft by Ebbe, who accuses him of being sympathetic towards the Germans. Werner is blown to bits after encountering landmines buried one above another and his twin brother Ernst goes to search for him and continues to deny his death even after being comforted by Rasmussen.
After a casual game of football, Rasmussen's dog is blown up in a supposedly cleared zone of the beach. This causes Rasmussen to snap and begin abusing the boys again. He forces them to march close together across the cleared zones of the beach to confirm that they are safe. When a young local girl walks out into an uncleared area of beach, her mother comes looking for Rasmussen only to find him gone. The boys volunteer to help save the girl. Ernst walks through the uncleared minefield to keep the little girl calm whilst Sebastian clears a path to safety for her. They manage to rescue her but instead of returning to safety with Sebastian, Ernst decides he cannot go on without his twin brother and commits suicide by walking backwards into the uncleared section and dies promptly.
After witnessing this act of kindness and bravery from the boys, Rasmussen relents in his treatment of them and reassures a grieving Sebastian that they will soon be able to go home. While four of the boys continue to clear the beach with Rasmussen, the rest of them are loading unexploded mines onto a truck. When one of the boys tosses a mine that was not properly defused onto the truckbed of deactivated mines, he accidentally sets off a massive chain reaction and kills himself and his comrades standing nearby. Only Sebastian, Ludwig, Helmut and Rodolf remain.
Although the boys had been promised that they would be sent home after defusing all of the mines, without Rasmussen's knowledge Jensen decides to send the surviving four to join a team defusing landmines without the aid of a map in another coastal area. He informs Rasmussen, who argues in vain for Jensen to rescind the order. Rasmussen decides to go against orders and rescues them, driving them within 500 metres of the German border and they obey his order to run to their freedom.
